subject.title: Poem ("When the immortal blond...")
subject.author: Robert Duncan
subject.text:
ROBERT DUNCAN

           A MORNING LETTER

The various members of the hierarchy move,
early morning awakening of the world.
They are like the shuffling of doors,
eager and reluctant, two-faced, I suppose.
Eight o'clock carillons seem universal magic.

Now after hoping for magic,
I was an ordinary messenger to arrive.
Wake up, you are yourself the God of Love
asleep. Whom did you expect? you lay
eyes closed as if afloat.
Proud boy,
whom did you expect who did not wear
only your lesser face? someone from up there?
someone just stepped down from a throne,
smelling of majesty?
Poetry has gone straight to your head.
Your mind wanders.
There are no empty thrones in heaven.
This is early morning in a world without kings.
A small-time Don Juan knocks at your door.
I put on all my pride to climb the stairs.

I was only messenger of myself
to tell you you are yourself Love.
How do you arrange the young men in your dreams?
arranging and re-arranging youth's hierarchies.
Don't you hear the bells ringing,
starting the day out with common tunes?

                                     ROBERT DUNCAN

Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay and Auld Lang Syne.
Waking up from your Imperial World,
you, for a moment, not I,
are Emperor of my world.
The hierarchies of powers move like doors
-this is a good dream figure.
Tam not dreaming.

I came to praise Love, not you.
And the poor writhe.
Bringing spiteful wreathes to celebrate. . . .
I, being poor, brought my pride.
Wake up from your Empire. I am still dreaming.
This is early morning in a world of kings.

      THE TEMPLE OF THE ANIMALS

The temple of the animals has fallen into disrepair.
The pad of feet has faded.
The panthers flee the shadows of the day.
The smell of musk has faded but lingers there-
lingers, lingers, Ah, bitterly in my room.
Tired, I recall the animals of last year:
the altars of the bear, tribunals of the ape,
solitudes of elephantine gloom, rare
zebra-striped retreats, prophecies of dog,
sanctuaries of the pygmy deer.

Were there rituals I had forgotten? animal calls
to which those animal voices replied,
calld and calld until that jungle stirrd.
Were there voices that I heard?

title: A Love Letter and a Ruined Temple, Filed Under a Third Poem's Name
standfirst: The text printed above this feature is not the poem its own title names. It is two shorter, correctly transcribed Robert Duncan poems from the same 1957 batch — one ranking lovers, one ranking animals — each built only to be pulled back down, while the poem actually called "When the immortal blond..." survives here as a title and nothing else.

sections.heading: Two Refrains That Cancel Each Other
sections.body:
Twenty-odd lines apart, the text above repeats itself with the opposite meaning. Early on: "There are no empty thrones in heaven. / This is early morning in a world without kings." Near the end, addressing the same half-asleep "you": "Wake up from your Empire. I am still dreaming. / This is early morning in a world of kings." Same hour, same room, same waking figure — and the world has acquired a monarchy it didn't have a moment ago.

That contradiction isn't a flaw. It's a seam, and seams are informative. The September 1957 issue of *Poetry* that carries this text lists five separate works under Robert Duncan's name: "A Morning Letter," "The Temple of the Animals," "There's Too Much Sea on the Big Sur," "Poem ("When the immortal blond...")," and "[A Ride to the Sea](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/27416/a-ride-to-the-sea)," according to the [issue's own table of contents](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/issue/70857/september-1957). The headline on this feature belongs to the fourth of those. What's printed above it is the first two, running on without a break — "A Morning Letter" straight into "The Temple of the Animals," bylines and all — exactly as the magazine's [own digitized page](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/27415/poem-when-the-immortal-blond) for "Poem" serves them up. Whatever "When the immortal blond..." actually says next is not recoverable from this entry; the line survives only as a fragment of a title, pointing at a scan of somebody else's poems.

Two short Duncan poems, then, correctly transcribed but wrongly filed. Read as what they actually are, they share one preoccupation closely enough that the misfiling does surprisingly little damage: both of them build a hierarchy, in loving detail, and then watch it fall apart.

sections.heading: A Proud Boy Promoted to Emperor
sections.body:
"A Morning Letter" opens by describing hierarchy as a physical fact of early morning, not a metaphor: "The various members of the hierarchy move, / early morning awakening of the world. / They are like the shuffling of doors, / eager and reluctant, two-faced, I suppose." Doors, not thrones — the ranking Duncan describes moves like furniture being used, not an order carved into anything. Into that scene comes a "messenger," addressing someone still asleep: "Wake up, you are yourself the God of Love / asleep." The address keeps testing how far up the ladder the sleeper can be pushed — "Proud boy, / whom did you expect who did not wear / only your lesser face? someone from up there? / someone just stepped down from a throne, / smelling of majesty?" — before undercutting the whole structure in the next breath: "There are no empty thrones in heaven. / This is early morning in a world without kings." The addressee is explicitly male and explicitly young: the poem goes on to ask him, "How do you arrange the young men in your dreams? / arranging and re-arranging youth's hierarchies." None of that needs inferring from outside the text — Duncan is describing a man ranking the men in his own dreaming, the way the morning itself ranks its doors.

The poem then performs a small demolition on its own device. A second voice — the page marks it with a repeated byline, "ROBERT DUNCAN," as though starting over — answers with vaudeville instead of myth: "Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay and Auld Lang Syne." (The following line is printed as "Tam not dreaming," which reads like a scanning slip for "I am not dreaming" rather than a Duncan coinage — this record is a photograph of a magazine page, and photographs of magazine pages misread letters.) Having spent twenty-odd lines promoting the sleeper from proud boy to "Emperor of my world," the speaker abruptly refuses the promotion he just handed out: "I came to praise Love, not you." The closing line reverses the poem's own refrain outright, "without kings" curdling into "a world of kings," and the reversal is the point. Duncan assembles a hierarchy out of mismatched parts — a popular tune jammed up against liturgical address — and then declines to stand at the top of it, or let anyone else stand there either.

sections.heading: A Court Gone to the Animals
sections.body:
Where "A Morning Letter" built its hierarchy out of courtiers and emperors, "The Temple of the Animals" builds the same shape out of a bestiary, and lets it rot. "The temple of the animals has fallen into disrepair. / The pad of feet has faded. / The panthers flee the shadows of the day." What follows is a one-sentence taxonomy of worship, each species given its own rank and its own furniture: "the altars of the bear, tribunals of the ape, / solitudes of elephantine gloom, rare / zebra-striped retreats, prophecies of dog, / sanctuaries of the pygmy deer." Bears get altars, apes get courts, dogs get prophecy — a complete, abandoned clergy. The poem ends on an unanswered question about whether any of it actually happened: "Were there rituals I had forgotten? animal calls / to which those animal voices replied, / calld and calld until that jungle stirrd. / Were there voices that I heard?"

Those last spellings — "calld," "stirrd" — are not errors to note and move past; they're Duncan's own habit. He clipped the silent *-ed* the same way in poems he kept and published as books: "This place rumord to have been Sodom" is the title of a piece he brought out three years later in *[The Opening of the Field](https://www.jacket2.org/article/robert-duncan-opening-field)*, spelled exactly that way in a rare-book dealer's [transcription of the finished volume's contents](https://www.abebooks.com/first-edition/Opening-Field-Duncan-Robert-Grove-Press/30410488536/bd). It's a small tell, but a real one: whoever wrote "calld" and "stirrd" in 1957 is recognizably the poet who kept doing it afterward. The habit suits the subject, too. An invented, faintly archaic spelling — English with its soft edges filed off — is exactly the register a reader raised, as Duncan was, on scripture and myth and horoscope read as the same kind of document might reach for: an ordinary word made to look older and more deliberate than it is, the way a ritual does.

sections.heading: Hierarchy Was Set Into Him Before Birth
sections.body:
Duncan did not come to hierarchy as an abstraction. He was born Edward Howard Duncan Jr. in Oakland on January 7, 1919; his mother died in the delivery. The couple who adopted him the following year, Edwin and Minnehaha Symmes, were [Theosophists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Duncan_%28poet%29), and the adoption came with conditions attached — among them that the child be received into the family at a time the Symmeses had set by consulting astrologers. Whatever the exact mechanics, the shape of the claim matches everything else known about the household: a family in which a person's place in the order of things was supposed to be legible in the stars before he had done anything at all to earn it. He was renamed Robert Edward Symmes, and did not take back the surname Duncan until 1941, in his early twenties.

As an adult he also attacked, in public and under his own name, the one hierarchy that had cost him the most directly. In 1944 the journal *politics* published his essay "The Homosexual in Society," years before any organization existed to make that kind of statement collectively. The consequence arrived fast and specific: John Crowe Ransom, who had accepted Duncan's poem "African Elegy" for the *Kenyon Review*, withdrew it once the essay appeared. A ranking system — which poets counted as serious, which men counted as normal — had just shown Duncan exactly how it enforced itself. "A Morning Letter," written thirteen years later, keeps circling the same move: hand someone a throne, then announce that heaven doesn't have any to spare. Only now he's the one doing the handing out, which heaven never offered to him.

sections.heading: A Household Instead of a Throne
sections.body:
By 1957 Duncan had already built, with the painter Jess Collins, an alternative to every hierarchy he'd grown up inside. They met in 1949 and exchanged private marriage vows in January 1951 that neither of them ever filed anywhere official, moving into a converted ballroom in a run-down Victorian the household nicknamed the Ghost House, where several tenants shared one bathroom. They called what they were building a household rather than a marriage, and Duncan was direct about why: "My whole idea of being able to work was to have a household," he said, in an exchange recounted in a [2020 piece on the two of them](https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2020/03/26/robert-duncan-jess-spirits-of-san-francisco/) in the *New York Review of Books*. By the back half of the 1950s the two were also keeping a home at [Stinson Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stinson_Beach%2C_California), up the coast from San Francisco, in the same years "A Morning Letter" and "The Temple of the Animals" went to press.

None of that is courtly language. It's the vocabulary of two equals running a house, set against a poem obsessed with who outranks whom inside somebody's dream. The gap between the two registers is exactly the gap "A Morning Letter" keeps falling into and climbing back out of — a writer who had built his actual domestic life as flat as he could make it, still reaching, on the page, for emperors and thrones and proud boys, if only for the pleasure of knocking them back down again.

sections.heading: Back From Black Mountain, Into a Door Rago Had Opened
sections.body:
Duncan arrived at this particular issue of *Poetry* by a specific route. In 1956, at Charles Olson's invitation, he had taught for a term at Black Mountain College in North Carolina, the school whose circle of [Black Mountain poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Mountain_poets) Olson led and gave an entire postwar current of American writing its name. The magazine that printed him the following September was, by then, a different magazine than it had been a few years earlier: Henry Rago took over as editor in 1955 and spent the next fourteen years publishing, in the words of his own [Poetry Foundation biography](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/henry-w-rago), "a wide range of poets, including the Black Mountain poets, Deep Image poets, and members of the New York School" — a generosity earlier editors had not reliably extended to Duncan's circle. Five Duncan poems in a single issue, this one included, is the kind of space only an editor actively making room would have handed over.

What became of that space afterward is harder to pin down than where it came from. *The Opening of the Field*, the book Duncan assembled from work written between 1956 and early 1959 — the same window this batch falls inside — does not appear to include any of the five. None of their titles turn up in the [dealer's transcription](https://www.abebooks.com/first-edition/Opening-Field-Duncan-Robert-Grove-Press/30410488536/bd) of the first edition's contents, and the standard division of his collected work falls on either side of 1957 without obviously picking it up: one volume runs through his 1953–56 book *Letters*, the next starts at 1958. Where that leaves these five poems, this record can't say for certain. What's certain is narrower and stranger: the one poem in the batch carrying this feature's own headline is also the one poem in it whose actual words, on this page, nobody gets to read.
